<reason>An unusually strong, symmetrical debate. A built a real path: "preferable" demands pricing the replacement, Vermont/Colorado show the honest invoice gets refused, and single-payer converts individual patchable risk into inescapable systemic risk. B never fully priced the transition, and A's execution was cleaner — B's Rebuttal 2 was clipped, a genuine cost. But B won the decisive ground. The motion indicts tying coverage to work status; A conceded that flaw and offered patches, and B showed the patches are either unaffordable (COBRA), poverty-gated (Medicaid), or — crucially — public financing. B's Q1 forced A to admit the sick non-worker's real exit is subsidized public coverage, and B's closing flipped that into the debate's cleanest kill: every door A offers opens into the same public-financing room, so the choice is public financing as floor or as trapdoor. B also met A's "name one real system" burden literally (Taiwan, South Korea) while A's dismissal of Taiwan was thin, and B defused Vermont accurately as a state-level rigged test (ERISA, federal tax subsidy, double bill) with Medicare's untouchability as counter-evidence. A's systemic-risk weighing stayed live but was matched by B's correlated-risk frame, which maps directly onto the motion's wording. B edged the two most important pressure exchanges and closed sharper.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Q1 plus the closing flip: pressing A to name a real exit for the 55-year-old whose cancer ended her ability to work, then converting A's own answer ("subsidized exchange coverage") into "every door CON offers opens into the same room — public financing," reframing the whole debate as floor versus trapdoor and turning CON's safety-net defense into PRO's mechanism.</best_rebuttal>
